chunks.text:
API Testing — Why test an API

An automated test is a small program that uses your API and checks that it behaves the
way you intended. You write it once and can run it again after every change.

Tests earn their keep in three ways. They **catch regressions**: when a later change
quietly breaks something that used to work, a failing test tells you before your users
do. They **document behaviour**: a test named "returns 404 when the task does not exist"
is a precise, always-up-to-date description of what the API promises. And they give you
**confidence to change code**, because you can check the whole API in seconds.

Trying an endpoint once in the browser and seeing it work is not proof. It shows one
request, with one set of data, on one day. It says nothing about bad input, missing
records, logged-out users, or whether it still works after next week's change.

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.text:
API Testing — What an API test checks

Almost every API test follows the same shape: send one HTTP request, then check the
response against what you expected. These checks are called **assertions**. If any
assertion is false, the test fails.

A good API test usually asserts on three things:

- **The status code.** Did a successful create return 201? Did a bad request return a
  4xx code rather than 200 or 500?
- **The response body.** Does the JSON contain the right fields and values? For an error,
  does it explain what went wrong?
- **Side effects.** Did the request change (or not change) the stored data as intended?
  After a successful `POST /tasks`, a follow-up `GET` should find the new task. After a
  rejected request, nothing should have been saved.

Checking only the status code is a common beginner gap: a 200 with the wrong data in the
body is still a bug.

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.section: The happy path and the failure cases
chunks.text:
API Testing — The happy path and the failure cases

The **happy path** is the case where everything is correct: a logged-in user sends valid
data for a resource that exists and that they own. It is the case you naturally try
first, and usually the one that already works.

Most bugs live in the **failure cases**, because they are easy to forget while building.
For almost any endpoint, ask these questions:

- **Invalid input:** what if a required field is missing, has the wrong type, or is too
  long?
- **Missing resource:** what if the id in the URL does not exist?
- **Not logged in:** what if the request has no token, or an expired one?
- **Someone else's resource:** what if a logged-in user asks for data that belongs to
  another user?

A useful rule of thumb: for each endpoint, write one happy-path test and at least one
test for each failure case that applies. A failure case should fail cleanly, with the
right 4xx status and a helpful error, never with a 500 or with someone else's data.

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.text:
API Testing — Unit, integration and end-to-end tests

Tests come in different sizes. Martin Fowler's **test pyramid** describes a healthy mix:

- **Unit tests** (bottom, the most): test one small piece of code, such as a function
  that checks whether a title is valid, without a server or database. They are fast and
  pinpoint exactly what broke.
- **Integration tests** (middle): test several pieces together, such as sending a real
  HTTP request to your API and letting it talk to a test database. Most of the API tests
  in this lesson are this kind.
- **End-to-end tests** (top, the fewest): test the whole system as a user would, for
  example through the real front end. They give the most realistic confidence but are
  slow and more fragile.

The shape is the point: many small fast tests, fewer bigger slow ones. If a behaviour can
be checked by a lower-level test, prefer that.

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.text:
API Testing — Arrange, act, assert

A clear test has three steps, often called **arrange, act, assert**:

1. **Arrange:** set up what the test needs (a user, a token, any existing data).
2. **Act:** send exactly one request.
3. **Assert:** check the status code, the body and any side effects.

Here is a happy-path test for creating a task, in plain pseudocode:

```
test "POST /tasks creates a task":
    # Arrange
    user  = create_test_user()
    token = log_in(user)

    # Act
    response = send POST /tasks
                 header Authorization: Bearer <token>
                 body   {"title": "Buy milk"}

    # Assert
    expect response.status == 201
    expect response.body.title == "Buy milk"
    expect response.body.id exists
    expect GET /tasks/<response.body.id> (as user) returns 200
```

Keeping one action per test means that when it fails, you know exactly which request
misbehaved.

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.text:
API Testing — Testing validation

Validation tests check that the API rejects bad input clearly and saves nothing. Your API
should pick one status code for invalid input and use it consistently; many APIs use
**400 Bad Request**, others use **422 Unprocessable Content**. The test should expect
whichever your API documents.

```
POST /tasks
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{}
```

Expected response:

```
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/json

{"errors": [{"field": "title", "message": "title is required"}]}
```

Assert on the status code, on the fact that the error names the **title** field, and that
no task was created. Then test the edges of each rule: if titles may be at most 200
characters, send 201 characters (expect rejection) and exactly 200 (expect success).
Bugs often hide right at the boundary.

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.text:
API Testing — Testing missing resources

When a request names a resource that does not exist, the API should say so with
**404 Not Found**, not crash with a 500 and not return 200 with an empty body.

```
GET /tasks/999
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

Expected:

```
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
```

To make this test reliable, the arrange step must guarantee that task 999 really does not
exist, for example by starting from an empty test database, or by creating a task,
deleting it, and then requesting its id.

The same check applies to every endpoint that takes an id: `PUT /tasks/999` and
`DELETE /tasks/999` should also return 404, and should not create or change anything.

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.text:
API Testing — Testing access control

Access control tests check who is allowed to do what. Two cases matter for almost every
endpoint:

- **No token (not authenticated):** send the request with no `Authorization` header.
  Expect **401 Unauthorized**.
- **Wrong user (not authorized):** user A logs in and requests a task owned by user B.
  Expect **403 Forbidden**, or **404 Not Found** if your API prefers not to reveal that
  the task exists. Either is fine if it is documented; 200 is never fine.

The second case catches **broken object level authorization (BOLA)**, the first item in
the OWASP API Security Top 10. It happens when the server checks that you are logged in
but forgets to check that the object you asked for is yours, so changing the id in the
URL exposes other people's data.

In the assert step, also check the side effect: after user A's rejected
`PUT /tasks/<B's id>`, user B's task must be unchanged.

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.text:
API Testing — Test data and isolation

Each test should **set up its own data** in its arrange step and should not rely on data
left behind by another test. Tests must pass in any order and when run on their own.

Why it matters: imagine test 1 creates a task and test 2 assumes that task exists. Run
test 2 alone, or run the tests in a different order, and it fails even though the API is
fine. Failures like this waste time and teach people to ignore red tests.

Common habits that keep tests isolated:

- Use a separate **test database**, never real production data.
- Reset or clean up data between tests, so each starts from a known state.
- Create fresh users and tasks inside each test, and use the ids you get back instead of
  hard-coding ids like 1 or 2.
- For access-control tests, create **two** users so you have a genuine "someone else".

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.text:
API Testing — Exercise: Write the test cases

You are testing `PUT /tasks/{id}` in a task API where every task has an owner. A valid
request body looks like `{"title": "Buy milk", "done": false}`, and a title is required.
List at least five test cases. For each one, write the request (who sends it, with what
token and body, to which id), the expected status code, and what else you would assert.
Your list must cover: a successful update, invalid input, a task that does not exist, a
request with no token, and a request for another user's task. For each failure case,
say what should be true about the stored task afterwards.

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.text:
API Testing — Exercise: Fix the flaky tests

A teammate's test file has two tests. Test A logs in as Alice and creates a task. Test B
logs in as Bob and sends `GET /tasks/1`, expecting 403 because "task 1 is Alice's". Test
B passes when the whole file runs, but fails when run on its own. Explain why it fails,
which testing principle it breaks, and rewrite Test B's arrange, act and assert steps so
it is reliable.

metadata.source: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html); OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/); MDN Web Docs — HTTP

chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — Authentication vs authorization

These two words sound alike but answer different questions.

- **Authentication** answers "who are you?" The server checks that you really are the
  person or program you claim to be, for example by checking a password.
- **Authorization** answers "what are you allowed to do?" Once the server knows who you
  are, it decides whether you may read, change or delete a particular thing.

Think of an office building. Your badge proves who you are: that is authentication. The
door rules decide which rooms your badge opens: that is authorization. Having a valid
badge does not mean every door opens for you.

Authentication always comes first, because you cannot decide what someone is allowed to
do until you know who they are. But passing authentication is only half the job. Many
real security bugs happen when a server checks *who* you are and then forgets to check
*what* you are allowed to touch.

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.section: How an API knows who you are
chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — How an API knows who you are

HTTP is stateless: the server does not remember you between requests. So the usual flow
is:

1. You log in once, for example by sending your email and password to `POST /login`.
2. If they are correct, the server gives you a credential: either a **session cookie**
   (a random ID the server links to your account) or a **token** (a string the server
   can verify, such as a signed JWT).
3. Your client sends that credential with **every** later request. A token usually goes
   in a header:

```
GET /users/123 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
```

4. On every request, the server verifies the credential and works out which user it
   belongs to. That user is the **authenticated user** for this request.

Credentials should only travel over HTTPS, so nobody on the network can copy them.

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.section: Passwords are never stored in plain text
chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — Passwords are never stored in plain text

A server must never save your actual password. If the database leaked, every password
would be exposed, and people reuse passwords on other sites. Instead the server stores a
**hash**: the result of a one-way function that turns the password into a fixed string
that cannot practically be turned back. At login, the server hashes the password you
typed and compares the result with the stored hash.

The hashing algorithm should be deliberately **slow** and **salted** (a random value is
mixed in for each user), so an attacker who steals the hashes cannot quickly try
billions of guesses. OWASP recommends algorithms built for this, such as **Argon2id** or
**bcrypt**. Fast general-purpose hashes like MD5 or plain SHA-256 are not suitable for
passwords.

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — 401 vs 403

Two status codes cover the two questions, and beginners often mix them up.

- **401 Unauthorized** means "I don't know who you are." The credential is missing,
  expired or invalid. Despite its name, 401 is about **authentication**. The fix for the
  client is to log in (again) and send a valid credential.
- **403 Forbidden** means "I know who you are, and you are not allowed to do this." The
  credential is fine, but the user lacks permission. This is about **authorization**.
  Logging in again will not help.

A quick test: if sending a valid login would fix the problem, it is a 401. If the user
is already logged in and still should not get in, it is a 403.

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.section: Authorization checks happen on the server, on every request
chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — Authorization checks happen on the server, on every request

The client — a browser, a mobile app, a script — is under the user's control. Anyone can
open developer tools, edit a URL, or send requests with a tool like `curl`, skipping
your app entirely. So the server must **never trust the client** to enforce rules.

Hiding a "Delete" button for regular users makes the UI nicer, but it is **not
security**. If the server accepts `DELETE /projects/7` from anyone who is logged in, an
attacker simply sends that request directly.

The rule from the OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet: enforce access control on the server,
check permissions on **every** request (not only the first one), and **deny by default**
— if no rule says the user is allowed, the answer is no.

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.section: Object-level authorization: does THIS user own THIS resource?
chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — Object-level authorization: does THIS user own THIS resource?

Here is a very common bug. A student logs in and opens their profile:

```
GET /users/123
Authorization: Bearer <student 123's token>
```

They notice the `123` in the URL, change it to `456`, and the server returns another
student's private data. The server checked that the token was valid (authentication
passed) but never checked whether user 123 is allowed to see user 456.

This is **Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)**, number one on the OWASP API
Security Top 10 2023 (API1:2023). It is also known as **IDOR** (Insecure Direct Object
Reference). It is common because APIs put object IDs right in the URL, and because each
endpoint needs its own check — forgetting one is easy.

The fix is an **object-level check**: on every request that touches a specific object,
the server asks "is the authenticated user allowed to access *this* object?"

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.section: The misconception: "hide or randomise the ID"
chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — The misconception: "hide or randomise the ID"

A common first reaction to the `/users/456` bug is "we should hide the user ID" or "use
random IDs so nobody can guess them". This does **not** fix the problem.

- IDs **leak**. They appear in links people share, browser history, server logs,
  screenshots, emails and other API responses.
- IDs get **guessed or collected**. Sequential numbers are trivial to guess, and even
  random ones can be found once they leak.
- Random IDs such as UUIDs make guessing **harder**, which is a reasonable extra layer,
  but OWASP is clear that unpredictable IDs are not a replacement for an authorization
  check.

Hiding the ID only makes the door harder to find. It does not lock it. The real fix is
always the same: the server checks, on every request, that the authenticated user is
allowed to access that specific resource.

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — Writing the check

The key idea: take the user's identity from the **verified credential**, never from the
URL or request body, then compare it with the resource.

Option 1, load then compare:

```
current_user = verify_token(request)        # 401 if missing or invalid
task = db.find_task(task_id)
if task is None:
    return 404
if task.owner_id != current_user.id:
    return 403   # or 404, see next section
return task
```

Option 2, put the check inside the query, so another user's row is never even loaded:

```sql
SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;
-- $1 = task id from the URL, $2 = id of the authenticated user
```

If no row comes back, the user either asked for something that does not exist or
something that is not theirs. Do the same for updates and deletes, not only for reads.

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — 403 or 404 for someone else's resource?

When a user asks for an object that exists but belongs to someone else, APIs use one of
two answers, and both are accepted practice:

- **403 Forbidden** is the literal meaning: "you are not allowed". It is clear and
  helpful when debugging.
- **404 Not Found** pretends the object is not there for this user. This avoids
  revealing that the object exists at all, which can matter when existence itself is
  sensitive (for example, whether an account exists).

Choose one approach and use it consistently. What matters far more than which code you
pick is that the data is **not returned**. Returning 200 with someone else's data is the
bug, whatever the code would otherwise have been.

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — Roles and permissions

Not every user is equal. A **role** groups permissions: an `admin` might be allowed to
delete any account, while a regular `student` may only edit their own profile.

Two kinds of checks work together:

- **Role (or function-level) checks** decide whether a user may perform an *action* at
  all: "only admins may call `DELETE /users/{id}`".
- **Ownership (object-level) checks** decide whether a user may act on a *specific
  object*: "a student may update `/tasks/42` only if task 42 is theirs".

A role check alone is not enough. Two students have the same role, yet neither should
read the other's tasks. Most endpoints need both: "is this kind of user allowed to do
this action?" and "is this user allowed to do it to this object?"

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.section: Exercise: Find the broken access control
chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — Exercise: Find the broken access control

A task-management API lets each user keep private to-do lists. User Alice (id 123) logs
in and receives a valid token. She calls `GET /users/123/tasks` and sees her tasks. Out
of curiosity she changes the URL to `GET /users/456/tasks`, sending the same token, and
receives `200 OK` with Bob's private tasks.

The server code for this endpoint verifies the token and then runs
`SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE user_id = <id from the URL>`.

Answer four questions: What exactly is wrong, and which authentication or authorization
step is missing? What check must the server perform, and where does the user's identity
for that check come from? What status code should Alice receive instead of 200? A
teammate suggests switching to random UUIDs instead of numbers — would that fix it?

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.text:
Authentication and Authorization — Exercise: Authentication or authorization?

For each situation, say whether it is an authentication problem or an authorization
problem, and which status code the API should return.

1. A request to `GET /me` arrives with no `Authorization` header at all.
2. A logged-in regular user calls `DELETE /users/88`, an endpoint only admins may use.
3. A user sends a token that expired yesterday.
4. A logged-in student requests `GET /grades/991`, which is another student's grade
   record.

metadata.source: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/); OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html); OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication

chunks.section: Why an API needs a database
chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — Why an API needs a database

An API server is a program, and anything it keeps in memory (a list in a variable, for
example) disappears when that program stops, crashes or is redeployed. Real data — users,
tasks, orders — has to outlive the server process, so the API stores it in a database.

A database also gives you one source of truth. Large APIs often run several copies of the
server at once behind a load balancer. If each copy kept its own in-memory list, a task
created through one copy would be invisible to the others. When every copy reads and
writes the same database, every request sees the same data.

In this lesson the database is a relational (SQL) database such as PostgreSQL. The API
receives an HTTP request, runs a query against the database, and turns the result into an
HTTP response.

metadata.source: PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD)

chunks.section: Tables, rows, columns and primary keys
chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — Tables, rows, columns and primary keys

A relational database stores data in **tables**. A table describes one kind of thing —
one resource. Each **column** is a named field with a type; each **row** is one record.

```sql
CREATE TABLE tasks (
    id         serial PRIMARY KEY,
    owner_id   integer NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    title      text NOT NULL,
    done       boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
```

| id | owner_id | title          | done  | created_at             |
|----|----------|----------------|-------|------------------------|
| 1  | 7        | Buy milk       | false | 2026-10-01 09:00:00+00 |
| 2  | 7        | Write report   | true  | 2026-10-02 14:30:00+00 |

The **primary key** (`id`) uniquely identifies each row: no two rows can share it and it
cannot be empty. `serial` makes the database pick the next number automatically. The
primary key is what appears in the URL: the row with `id = 2` is the resource
`/tasks/2`.

metadata.source: PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD)

chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete

Almost everything an API does to stored data is one of four operations, known as
**CRUD**. Each maps to one SQL statement.

```sql
-- Create: add a new row
INSERT INTO tasks (owner_id, title) VALUES (7, 'Buy milk');

-- Read: fetch rows
SELECT id, title, done FROM tasks WHERE id = 1;

-- Update: change columns of existing rows
UPDATE tasks SET done = true WHERE id = 1;

-- Delete: remove rows
DELETE FROM tasks WHERE id = 1;
```

Notice the `WHERE` clause on SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE. It chooses which rows the
statement affects. An `UPDATE` or `DELETE` with no `WHERE` applies to **every row in the
table** — a classic and painful mistake.

In PostgreSQL you can add `RETURNING` to INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE to get the affected
row back, for example `INSERT ... RETURNING id, title, done, created_at;`. That is handy
for sending the created resource in the response.

metadata.source: PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD)

chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — Mapping REST endpoints to CRUD

Each REST endpoint for a resource lines up with one CRUD operation and one SQL statement.
`$1`, `$2` are placeholders the server fills with real values (see parameterized
queries below).

```
POST   /tasks       Create  INSERT INTO tasks (owner_id, title)
                            VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING *            -> 201 Created
GET    /tasks       Read    SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = $1 -> 200 OK
GET    /tasks/{id}  Read    SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE id = $1      -> 200 OK
PATCH  /tasks/{id}  Update  UPDATE tasks SET done = $1
                            WHERE id = $2 RETURNING *              -> 200 OK (or 204)
DELETE /tasks/{id}  Delete  DELETE FROM tasks WHERE id = $1        -> 204 No Content
```

PUT maps to UPDATE too; it just sets every editable column instead of a few. Return 200
with the updated task in the body, or 204 if you send no body. A 201 usually includes
the new task and a `Location: /tasks/{id}` header.

metadata.source: PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD)

chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — When the row doesn't exist

A client can ask for an id that was never created or was already deleted. The database
does not treat this as an error — the query simply matches nothing — so the API must
check and respond with **404 Not Found**.

- `SELECT ... WHERE id = $1` returns **zero rows** → respond 404.
- `UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1` or `DELETE ... WHERE id = $1` reports **0 rows affected**
  → respond 404. Database drivers expose this as a row count (for example
  `cursor.rowcount` in Python), or you can use `RETURNING` and check whether a row came
  back.

A common bug is to run the UPDATE, ignore the row count, and return 200 anyway. The client
then believes it changed a task that does not exist.

metadata.source: PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD)

chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — Relationships and foreign keys

Resources are related: every task belongs to a user. Instead of copying the user's name
and email into each task, the `tasks` table stores the user's primary key in an
`owner_id` column.

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
    id    serial PRIMARY KEY,
    email text NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
-- in tasks:  owner_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id)
```

`REFERENCES users(id)` makes `owner_id` a **foreign key**. The database then refuses to
insert a task whose `owner_id` does not match an existing user, and by default refuses to
delete a user who still has tasks. This is called referential integrity.

The `owner_id` column is also what makes authorization possible later: to decide whether
a request may see or change a task, the API compares the task's `owner_id` with the id of
the logged-in user.

metadata.source: PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD)

chunks.section: Filtering by owner: the "my tasks" query
chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — Filtering by owner: the "my tasks" query

A "my tasks" endpoint such as `GET /tasks` must return only the tasks of the user making
the request, never everyone's. The server takes the user id from the authenticated
request (not from a value the client can freely edit) and filters on it:

```sql
SELECT id, title, done, created_at
FROM tasks
WHERE owner_id = $1
ORDER BY created_at DESC;
```

The same idea protects single-task endpoints. Adding the owner to the `WHERE` clause means
another user's task simply isn't found:

```sql
SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;
UPDATE tasks SET done = $1 WHERE id = $2 AND owner_id = $3;
DELETE FROM tasks WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;
```

If this returns no row, the API can respond 404, which also avoids revealing that the
task exists. Forgetting the owner filter is one of the most common API security bugs.

metadata.source: PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD)

chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — Parameterized queries vs string concatenation

Never build SQL by gluing user input into a string. Suppose the server does this
(Python):

```python
# BAD: user input becomes part of the SQL text
sql = "SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE title = '" + title + "'"
```

If a client sends the title `x' OR '1'='1`, the query becomes
`SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE title = 'x' OR '1'='1'`, which matches every row in the table.
Cleverer inputs can read other tables or delete data. This attack is **SQL injection**.

Use a **parameterized query** instead: the SQL text contains placeholders, and the values
are sent to the database separately.

```python
# GOOD: the value is passed separately and never parsed as SQL
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE title = %s", (title,))
```

The placeholder style depends on the driver (`%s` in psycopg, `$1` in node-postgres and
asyncpg), but the rule is the same: the database treats the value only as data, so
quotes and SQL keywords inside it are harmless.

metadata.source: PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD)

chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — Unique constraints and 409 Conflict

Some columns must never repeat — two accounts cannot share an email. Declaring the column
`UNIQUE` makes the database enforce this:

```sql
email text NOT NULL UNIQUE
```

If `POST /users` tries to insert an email that already exists, the INSERT fails with a
unique-violation error (SQLSTATE `23505` in PostgreSQL). The API should catch that
specific error and respond **409 Conflict** with a clear message such as
"email already registered" — not let it bubble up as a 500, which wrongly says the
server is broken.

Checking first with a SELECT and then inserting is not enough on its own: two requests
can both see "no such email" and both insert. The constraint is the reliable guard,
because the database checks it at the moment of the write.

metadata.source: PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD)
PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD)

chunks.section: Exercise: Back the task API with a table
chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — Exercise: Back the task API with a table

You are given this table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE tasks (
    id       serial PRIMARY KEY,
    owner_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    title    text NOT NULL,
    done     boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false
);
```

The logged-in user's id is available to the server. For each of these four endpoints,
write the SQL query it should run (use `$1`, `$2` placeholders, not pasted-in values),
the status code on success, and the status code when the task doesn't exist:

1. `POST /tasks` with body `{"title": "Buy milk"}`
2. `GET /tasks/{id}`
3. `PATCH /tasks/{id}` with body `{"done": true}`
4. `DELETE /tasks/{id}`

Then explain in one or two sentences how your server knows that the task in 2–4 didn't
exist, and why your queries should also mention `owner_id`.

chunks.section: Exercise: Spot the bugs in a signup endpoint
chunks.text:
Databases and CRUD — Exercise: Spot the bugs in a signup endpoint

A teammate wrote `POST /users` like this:

```python
sql = "INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('" + body["email"] + "')"
cur.execute(sql)
return 201
```

The `email` column is `UNIQUE`. When someone signs up twice with the same email, the
client receives `500 Internal Server Error`. Name two problems with this code, explain
what could go wrong with each, and say what status code a duplicate signup should
return and how the server should detect it.

chunks.section: Clients, servers and the request–response cycle
chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — Clients, servers and the request–response cycle

On the web, two programs talk to each other. The **client** is the program asking for
something: a browser, a mobile app, or another program. The **server** is a program
running on another computer that waits for requests and answers them.

Think of a restaurant. You (the client) place an order with the waiter. The kitchen (the
server) prepares it. The waiter brings back your dish, or tells you it is unavailable.

HTTP maps onto this precisely:

- **Your order is the HTTP request.** It says what you want to do (the method, such as
  `GET`), which thing you want (the path, such as `/menu/soup`), extra details (headers)
  and sometimes data (the body).
- **The kitchen's work is server processing.** The server reads the request, looks up or
  changes data, and decides how to answer.
- **What the waiter brings back is the HTTP response.** It has a status code saying how
  it went (`200 OK`, `404 Not Found`), headers, and usually a body with the data.

Each exchange is one request, then one response. The client always speaks first.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status); MDN Web Docs — How the web works (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works); RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics

chunks.section: What happens when you type a web address
chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — What happens when you type a web address

Say you type `https://example.com/news` into your browser and press Enter.

1. **Find the server (DNS).** Computers find each other by numeric IP addresses, not
   names. The browser asks DNS, the internet's phone book, for the IP
   address of `example.com`.
2. **Connect.** The browser opens a network connection to that address. Because the
   address starts with `https`, the connection is also encrypted.
3. **Send a request.** The browser sends an HTTP request such as `GET /news`, meaning
   "please give me the page at `/news`".
4. **Get a response.** The server replies with a status code (for example `200 OK`),
   headers (for example `Content-Type: text/html`) and a body containing the page's HTML.
5. **Render.** The browser reads the HTML and draws the page. If the page needs images,
   styles or scripts, the browser sends more requests for each of them.

An app calling an API follows the same steps, except the body is usually data (often
JSON) for the app to display, instead of a page for the browser to draw.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status); MDN Web Docs — How the web works (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works); RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — What an HTTP request is

HTTP is a request/response protocol. A client sends a request to a server, the server
returns a response, and the connection concern ends there. Every request carries four
things: a method, a path, a set of headers, and an optional body.

A minimal request looks like this:

```
GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json
```

The method says what the client wants to do. The path identifies the resource. Headers
carry metadata such as content type, authentication and caching directives. The body
carries data, and is empty for methods like GET.

HTTP is stateless. The server does not remember anything about a previous request from
the same client. Any continuity — a login session, a shopping cart — has to be carried
explicitly in each request, usually in a cookie or an Authorization header.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status); MDN Web Docs — How the web works (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works); RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — HTTP methods

GET retrieves a resource and must not change server state. POST submits data and
typically creates something. PUT replaces a resource entirely. PATCH modifies part of a
resource. DELETE removes it.

Two properties matter when reasoning about methods. A method is **safe** if it does not
modify state: GET is safe, POST is not. A method is **idempotent** if making the same
request many times has the same effect as making it once: GET, PUT and DELETE are
idempotent, POST is not. Idempotency is why a client can safely retry a failed PUT but
not a failed POST — retrying a POST may create a duplicate record.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status); MDN Web Docs — How the web works (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works); RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — Status codes

Every response starts with a three-digit status code, grouped by its first digit.

- **2xx — success.** The request worked.
- **3xx — redirection.** The client should look elsewhere. 301 is a permanent move, 302
  a temporary one. 304 Not Modified tells the client its cached copy is still valid.
- **4xx — client error.** Something is wrong with the request itself.
- **5xx — server error.** The request may be fine, but the server failed to handle it.

The 4xx/5xx split matters operationally: 4xx means the client must change something
before trying again, 5xx means the server is at fault and the client may reasonably
retry later.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status); MDN Web Docs — How the web works (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works); RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — Common success codes

- **200 OK** — the request succeeded; the body holds the result (for example, the user
  you asked for).
- **201 Created** — a new resource was created, typically after a POST; the response
  often includes the new resource and a `Location` header with its URL.
- **204 No Content** — the request succeeded and there is nothing to send back, common
  after a DELETE.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status); MDN Web Docs — How the web works (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works); RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — Common error codes

- **400 Bad Request** — the request is malformed or invalid, such as broken JSON or a
  missing required field.
- **401 Unauthorized** — the client is not authenticated: no credentials, or invalid
  ones. Despite the name, it means "we don't know who you are".
- **403 Forbidden** — the client is authenticated, but is not allowed to do this. "We
  know who you are, and the answer is no."
- **404 Not Found** — the requested resource does not exist on the server.
- **409 Conflict** — the request conflicts with the current state of the resource, such
  as creating an account with an email that is already registered.
- **429 Too Many Requests** — the client is sending too many requests and is rate
  limited.
- **500 Internal Server Error** — an unexpected failure on the server, such as a bug or
  crash. 502 Bad Gateway and 503 Service Unavailable usually indicate a problem
  upstream or an overloaded service.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status); MDN Web Docs — How the web works (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works); RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — Headers and content negotiation

Headers let client and server agree on the shape of the exchange without changing the
URL. `Accept` tells the server what formats the client can handle; `Content-Type` tells
the receiver what format the body actually is. `Authorization` carries credentials.
`Cache-Control` governs how long a response may be reused.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status); MDN Web Docs — How the web works (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works); RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — Exercise: Read a failing request

A client repeatedly sends `POST /orders` and receives `500 Internal Server Error`. The
client retries automatically five times. Answer three questions: Is it safe for the
client to retry this request? What would change if the endpoint returned 400 instead?
What single property of POST makes the retry risky here?

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status); MDN Web Docs — How the web works (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works); RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — Exercise: Choose the status code

You are building the API for a small library app. For each situation below, say which
HTTP status code the server should return, and explain in one sentence why.

1. A logged-in librarian sends `POST /books` with a valid new book, and the server saves
   it.
2. A visitor who has not logged in sends `DELETE /books/12`.
3. A logged-in student (not a librarian) sends `DELETE /books/12`, but only librarians
   may delete books.
4. Someone sends `GET /books/9999`, and no book with id 9999 exists.

Bonus: in situation 3, why would 401 be the wrong answer?

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status); MDN Web Docs — How the web works (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works); RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics

chunks.text:
REST API Design — What a REST API is

An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is a way for one program to ask another
for data or actions. A **REST API** is a style of web API built on plain HTTP, organised
around **resources**: the nouns of your system, such as tasks, users or orders.

- Each resource has a **URL**. `/tasks` is the collection of all tasks; `/tasks/7` is
  the one task with id 7.
- The **HTTP method** is the verb: what you want to do to that resource.
- Data travels as a **representation** of the resource, usually **JSON**, such as
  `{"id": 7, "title": "Buy milk", "done": false}`.

A to-do app's task API looks like this:

```
GET    /tasks        list all tasks
POST   /tasks        create a new task (body: the task's data)
GET    /tasks/{id}   fetch one task
PUT    /tasks/{id}   replace that task completely
PATCH  /tasks/{id}   change part of that task
DELETE /tasks/{id}   delete that task
```

`{id}` is a placeholder for a real id, such as `/tasks/7`. Notice that only two URLs
are needed: the method, not the path, says what happens.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5; RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics; RFC 5789 PATCH Method for HTTP; RFC 7396 JSON Merge Patch; MDN Web Docs — HTTP request methods (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods)

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Resources and URL structure

A REST API models a system as a set of **resources**, each addressable by a URL. The
central design move is that URLs name things, not actions. `/users/42/orders` is a
resource. `/getUserOrders?id=42` is a remote procedure call wearing a URL costume.

Conventional structure uses plural nouns and nests to show ownership:

```
GET    /orders          list orders
POST   /orders          create an order
GET    /orders/42       fetch one order
PATCH  /orders/42       modify part of it
DELETE /orders/42       remove it
GET    /users/7/orders  orders belonging to user 7
```

The verb lives in the HTTP method, never in the path. If you find yourself writing
`/orders/42/cancel`, the question to ask is whether cancellation is really a state
change on the order (`PATCH /orders/42` with `{"status":"cancelled"}`) or genuinely a
new resource (`POST /orders/42/cancellations`). Both are defensible; `/cancel` as a verb
in the path is the option that breaks the model.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5; RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics; RFC 5789 PATCH Method for HTTP; RFC 7396 JSON Merge Patch; MDN Web Docs — HTTP request methods (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods)

chunks.text:
REST API Design — PUT vs PATCH

Both update an existing resource, but in different ways. Suppose task 7 is currently:

```json
{ "id": 7, "title": "Buy milk", "done": false, "due": "2026-10-20" }
```

**PUT replaces the whole representation.** The client sends the complete new version:

```
PUT /tasks/7
{ "title": "Buy oat milk", "done": false, "due": "2026-10-20" }
```

Any field left out is treated as gone: had the client omitted `due`, the task would end
up with no due date. PUT is **idempotent**: sending the same PUT five times leaves the
task in exactly the same state as sending it once, so it is safe to retry.

**PATCH applies a partial change.** The client sends only what should change:

```
PATCH /tasks/7
{ "done": true }
```

The title and due date stay as they were. (This body format, "send only the fields to
change", is called JSON Merge Patch and is a common convention.) PATCH is not guaranteed
to be idempotent, though simple "set this field" patches like this one are in practice.

Rule of thumb: PATCH to change a field or two; PUT to replace the whole resource.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5; RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics; RFC 5789 PATCH Method for HTTP; RFC 7396 JSON Merge Patch; MDN Web Docs — HTTP request methods (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods)

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Request and response design

Responses should be predictable in shape. A collection endpoint returns a list plus
pagination metadata; a single-resource endpoint returns the object. Keeping the envelope
consistent means clients can write one parsing path instead of one per endpoint.

Errors deserve as much design attention as success cases. An error response should carry
a machine-readable code, a human-readable message, and enough context to act on:

```json
{ "error": { "code": "insufficient_stock",
             "message": "Only 2 units of SKU-119 remain",
             "field": "items[0].quantity" } }
```

Returning `200 OK` with `{"success": false}` is a common mistake. It forces every client
to inspect the body to learn whether the call worked, and it defeats every piece of
infrastructure — proxies, monitoring, retry logic — that reasons about status codes.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5; RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics; RFC 5789 PATCH Method for HTTP; RFC 7396 JSON Merge Patch; MDN Web Docs — HTTP request methods (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods)

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Versioning

Any API with external consumers will need to change incompatibly at some point.
Versioning in the path (`/v1/orders`) is the most common approach because it is visible,
easy to route, and easy to reason about in logs. Header-based versioning keeps URLs
stable but makes debugging harder because the version is invisible in a browser.

The important discipline is distinguishing breaking from non-breaking changes. Adding an
optional field is non-breaking. Removing a field, renaming one, or tightening validation
is breaking and needs a new version.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5; RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics; RFC 5789 PATCH Method for HTTP; RFC 7396 JSON Merge Patch; MDN Web Docs — HTTP request methods (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods)

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Pagination

Returning an unbounded list is a latency and memory problem waiting to happen.
**Offset pagination** (`?limit=20&offset=40`) is simple but degrades on large offsets,
because the database must still walk past every skipped row, and it can skip or repeat
items when rows are inserted between requests.

**Cursor pagination** (`?limit=20&after=eyJpZCI6NDJ9`) passes an opaque pointer to the
last item seen. It stays fast at any depth and is stable under concurrent inserts, at the
cost of not being able to jump to an arbitrary page.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5; RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics; RFC 5789 PATCH Method for HTTP; RFC 7396 JSON Merge Patch; MDN Web Docs — HTTP request methods (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods)

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Exercise: Critique an endpoint

An API exposes `POST /api/getUsersByStatus` which accepts `{"status": "active"}` and
returns `200 OK` with `{"success": true, "data": [...]}` — all 40,000 matching users.
List four separate design problems with this endpoint and give the corrected version of
each. State which single change you would make first and why.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5; RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics; RFC 5789 PATCH Method for HTTP; RFC 7396 JSON Merge Patch; MDN Web Docs — HTTP request methods (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods)

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Exercise: Design a profile API

A university app stores one profile per student, with fields such as `name`, `email`
and `programme`. Design the REST endpoints for these five operations. For each, give
the HTTP method, the path, and the status code the server returns on success:

1. Retrieve a student's profile.
2. Create a new profile.
3. Replace a profile completely with new data.
4. Update just the student's email address.
5. Delete a profile.

Finally: what should the API return if a client asks to retrieve, update or delete a
profile that does not exist? Explain why that is better than returning `200 OK` with an
error message in the body.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5; RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics; RFC 5789 PATCH Method for HTTP; RFC 7396 JSON Merge Patch; MDN Web Docs — HTTP request methods (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods)

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — Never trust input

Everything that arrives in a request comes from the client: the body, the path, query
parameters and headers. The server cannot control any of it. A person can mistype, a
buggy app can send the wrong shape, and an attacker can send whatever they like using a
tool such as curl, skipping your website entirely.

So the rule is simple: treat all input as untrusted until the server has checked it.

Checks in the browser or mobile app (client-side validation) are still useful. They give
the user instant feedback, like "please enter your email", without a round trip. But
they are a convenience, not protection, because anyone can bypass the client and call
the API directly. The server must repeat every check that matters.

metadata.source: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics — status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110); RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457); OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — What to validate

For each field the server accepts, decide what "valid" means and check it:

- **Required fields** — is it present at all? A task without a title makes no sense.
- **Type** — is `title` a string, is `priority` a number, is `done` a true/false value?
- **Length and range** — a title of 1–200 characters; an age of 0–150, not -5.
- **Format** — does an email look like an email, is a date a real date?
- **Allowed values** — `status` must be one of `"todo"`, `"doing"` or `"done"`.

Example rules for creating a task:

```
title     required, string, 1-200 characters
status    optional, one of "todo" | "doing" | "done", default "todo"
due_date  optional, a valid date such as "2026-03-01"
```

Where possible, describe what is allowed (an allowlist) rather than trying to list every
bad input. OWASP recommends allowlists because the list of bad inputs is never complete.

metadata.source: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics — status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110); RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457); OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

chunks.section: Validate early on the server and reject bad input
chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — Validate early on the server and reject bad input

Run validation at the start of the request handler, before you save anything or call
other services. If the input is invalid, stop and return an error response. Nothing
should be half-written to the database.

Do not silently "fix" bad input. If a client sends `"age": -5`, quietly changing it to
`0`, or cutting a 500-character title down to 200, hides a bug in the client and stores
data the user never meant. Reject it and say what is wrong, so the client can correct it.

Light, predictable normalisation is fine when it is part of your documented rules, for
example trimming spaces around a title before checking its length. The difference is
that the rule is published and consistent, not a guess about what the client meant.

metadata.source: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics — status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110); RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457); OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — 400 Bad Request vs 422 Unprocessable Content

Two status codes are used for bad input, and they mean slightly different things.

**400 Bad Request** means the server could not process the request because it is
malformed. A classic case is a body that is not valid JSON at all:

```
{"title": "Buy milk",
```

**422 Unprocessable Content** means the request is well-formed — the JSON parses fine —
but the values break the rules. For example `{"title": ""}` is valid JSON, but an empty
title is not allowed.

In practice, many APIs use 400 for both cases, and that is a common, acceptable choice.
Other APIs (and frameworks such as FastAPI) use 422 for validation failures. Either way,
the key points are: use a 4xx code, because the client must change the request, and be
consistent across your whole API.

metadata.source: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics — status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110); RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457); OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — 404, 409 and 405

A few other 4xx codes cover common situations.

**404 Not Found** — the resource does not exist. `GET /tasks/999` when there is no task
999 returns 404. It is also correct for `PATCH` or `DELETE` on a task that does not exist.

**409 Conflict** — the request conflicts with the current state of the resource. A common
example is trying to create something that must be unique and already exists, such as
signing up with a username that is already taken.

**405 Method Not Allowed** — the URL exists but does not support that method, such as
`DELETE /tasks` when the API does not allow deleting the whole collection. A 405 response
must include an `Allow` header listing the methods that are supported, for example
`Allow: GET, POST`.

metadata.source: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics — status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110); RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457); OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — 500 errors: unexpected failures

**500 Internal Server Error** means something went wrong on the server that was not the
client's fault: the database is down, a bug threw an exception, a dependency crashed. The
client did nothing wrong, so this belongs in the 5xx range, not 4xx.

When this happens, never send the internal details to the client. A stack trace, an SQL
error message, file paths or library versions tell an attacker how your system is built
and help them find weaknesses. They also mean nothing to a normal user.

Instead:

- **Log** the full error on the server, with enough detail to debug it later.
- **Return** a short, generic message, for example "An unexpected error occurred".
- Optionally include a request or error ID, so a user can report it and you can find the
  matching log entry.

metadata.source: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics — status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110); RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457); OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — A good error response body

Error bodies should have one consistent JSON shape across the whole API, so clients can
handle every error with the same code. RFC 9457, "Problem Details for HTTP APIs", defines
a standard shape, sent with the content type `application/problem+json`:

```json
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/validation-error",
  "title": "Your request contains invalid fields",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "2 fields failed validation.",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "title", "message": "Title is required." },
    { "field": "status", "message": "Must be one of: todo, doing, done." }
  ]
}
```

`type` is a URI identifying the kind of problem, `title` a short summary, `status` the
HTTP status code, and `detail` an explanation of this specific occurrence. RFC 9457 also
allows extra members, so a list of field-level errors like `errors` is a common addition.

metadata.source: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics — status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110); RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457); OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

chunks.section: Error messages that help without leaking
chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — Error messages that help without leaking

A good error message tells the client exactly what to fix: which field is wrong and why.
"Title must be 1–200 characters" is useful. "Invalid input" or `{"error": "bad"}` is not.

But helpful must not become revealing. Some details help attackers more than users:

- **Login:** say "Invalid email or password" whether the email is unknown or the password
  is wrong. Saying "No account with this email" lets anyone discover who has an account.
- **Internals:** no stack traces, SQL, table names or server paths in messages.
- **Echoing input:** be careful repeating the client's raw input back, especially into
  web pages, where it could be used to inject scripts.

A good test: would this message help a legitimate user fix their request, without
teaching an attacker anything about your system or your users?

metadata.source: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics — status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110); RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457); OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — Missing resources vs empty results

Two situations look similar but get different answers.

**A specific resource that does not exist.** `GET /tasks/42` when there is no task 42 is
an error: the client asked for one thing and it is not there. Return **404 Not Found**.

**A collection that happens to be empty.** `GET /tasks` when the user has no tasks yet is
not an error. The collection `/tasks` exists; it just has nothing in it. Return
**200 OK** with an empty list:

```json
{ "items": [] }
```

The same goes for a search or filter with no matches, such as
`GET /tasks?status=done`: 200 with an empty list. Returning 404 here would make clients
treat a normal situation as a failure, and they could not tell "no tasks" apart from a
wrong URL.

metadata.source: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics — status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110); RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457); OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — Exercise: Fix the error responses

A to-do API has an endpoint `POST /tasks`. The title is required and must be 1–200
characters. The endpoint behaves like this:

1. When the client sends `{}` (no title), it returns **200 OK** with the body
   `{"error": "bad"}`.
2. When the database is down, it returns **500 Internal Server Error** with a body
   containing the full stack trace, including the line
   `psycopg.OperationalError: connection to server at "10.0.3.7", port 5432 failed`.

For each case, explain what is wrong with the current response, and describe what the
status code and the response body should be instead.

metadata.source: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics — status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110); RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457); OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Handling — Exercise: Pick the right response

For each request to a to-do API, choose the status code and briefly say why:

1. `GET /tasks/999`, and there is no task 999.
2. `GET /tasks`, and the user has no tasks yet.
3. `POST /tasks` with the body `{"title": "Buy milk",` (cut off, not valid JSON).
4. `POST /tasks` with `{"title": "Buy milk", "status": "maybe"}`, where status must be
   `todo`, `doing` or `done`.
5. `POST /users` with a username that is already taken.
